summary: States the problem of letting many systems talk directly to each other over IPsec when setting up every tunnel by hand is too burdensome, endpoint addresses change, or NAT gets in the way. It then lists requirements for an Auto-Discovery VPN solution that would set up such tunnels dynamically.

plainLanguage.summary: If lots of offices each need a private tunnel to every other office, setting them all up by hand is a mess. This asks for a system that builds the tunnels as needed.

questions: dynamic ipsec tunnels between many sites

subtitle: Why hand-configuring IPsec tunnels between many sites does not scale, and what a dynamic fix must do.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs a lot of per-tunnel configuration, so connecting hundreds of thousands of gateways and endpoints directly to one another by hand is not practical, especially when addresses change or NAT is involved.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three use cases, explains why exhaustive configuration, star topologies and proprietary products fall short, and lists 16 requirements that an Auto-Discovery VPN (ADVPN) solution should meet.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement only. It defines no protocol, and it warns that letting a protocol update IPsec policy databases needs a clear trust model.

facts.label: Topologies covered
facts.value: Star, full mesh, dynamic full mesh

facts.label: Scale motivating the work
facts.value: Hundreds of thousands of gateways and endpoints

today: RFC 7018 is an Informational document and is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It states a problem and requirements rather than a protocol, so it contains nothing to implement directly.

sections.title: The Large-Scale IPsec Problem
sections.content:
IPsec is used for tunnel-mode site-to-site VPNs and remote access VPNs. This RFC covers both tunneling modes for IPsec gateways and host-to-host transport mode. Its subject is what goes wrong in large deployments: many gateways connecting sites, many remote endpoints connecting to gateways or to each other, or a mix. The participants may share one administrative domain or several domains with a trust relationship.

The pain comes from the databases described in Section 4.4 of RFC 4301. Each tunnel needs extensive configuration to set up a Security Association. IKE implementations must know the identity and credentials of every possible peer, plus the addresses of the hosts and networks behind them. The RFC concludes that a simplified mechanism for dynamically establishing point-to-point tunnels is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every tunnel needs its own long list of settings. With a huge number of offices, writing all those lists by hand is not realistic.

sections.title: Terminology and Topologies
sections.content:
An Auto-Discovery VPN (ADVPN) lets a large number of systems communicate directly, with minimal configuration and operator intervention, using IPsec. An endpoint uses IPsec for its own traffic; a gateway protects traffic flowing through it. A hub is a gateway that other hubs or spokes connect to. A spoke is an endpoint or a gateway that forwards traffic from cleartext devices to other hubs or spokes.

Three topologies matter. In a star topology there is direct connectivity only between hub and spoke, so two spokes talk through the hub. In a full mesh every spoke connects directly to every other spoke. In a dynamic full mesh the hub-and-spoke connections exist, but direct spoke-to-spoke connections are created and removed as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A star is like a bus station where every trip changes buses in the middle. A full mesh is a road between every pair of towns. A dynamic mesh builds the direct road only when people actually want to travel it.

sections.title: The Three Use Cases
sections.content:
Endpoint-to-endpoint: two endpoints want a secure point-to-point SA, for example two nearby users making a video or voice call without routing it through remote gateways that add latency and cost. It should also work when both are behind NAT gateways and as endpoints roam. In a star topology, the two endpoints need authentication that does not expose them to impersonation by the other spoke.

Gateway-to-gateway: enterprise traffic usually follows a star, but rich media sent through the hub causes bottlenecks and cost (the RFC calls this traffic tromboning). A full mesh avoids this but needs considerable configuration, so spoke-to-spoke tunnels should be created and torn down dynamically. The solution should handle dynamic gateway addresses, GRE and OSPF running over IPsec, and Layer 3 VPNs.

Endpoint-to-gateway: a roaming mobile endpoint should be able to discover and move to the most efficient gateway without bringing down its connection. Establishing communication between parties with no established trust relationship is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Two friends in the same room should be able to call each other directly instead of through a far-away office. A traveling phone should switch to the nearest office without dropping the call.

sections.title: Why Existing Solutions Fall Short
sections.content:
Exhaustive configuration means preloading every gateway and endpoint with everything needed to reach every other. It does not scale to hundreds of thousands of systems, particularly across administrative domains and with mobile endpoints, and it is limited by the smallest device.

The star topology is the most common answer today, but it is complicated when spokes have dynamic IP addresses, and it puts high load on the hub gateways and on the links to them. A single packet can be encrypted and decrypted several times. The RFC's example is two remote users in the same building on fast WiFi whose conversation is channeled through their employers' hubs.

Proprietary approaches exist, but they do not interoperate between vendors, which keeps them within one organization and makes it harder to move away from them.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing every route by hand is too much work. Sending everything through one middle office makes a traffic jam. Special systems from one company do not work with another company's.

sections.title: The 16 Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4.1 lists 16 requirements. The strongest (MUST) ones are:

  • Adding or removing a spoke MUST NOT require configuration changes in other spokes, or in hubs other than the one the spoke connected to.
  • Peers MUST be able to set up tunnels without configuration changes even when peer addresses change every time a device comes up.
  • Tunneling and routing protocols such as GRE and OSPF MUST work over spoke-to-spoke tunnels with minimal or no configuration impact.
  • In full-mesh and dynamic full-mesh topologies spokes MUST be able to talk directly; in star mode direct spoke communication MUST be disallowed.
  • No peer MAY be able to obtain another peer's long-term authentication credentials, and compromise of an endpoint MUST NOT affect other peers' communications.
  • Gateways and endpoints MUST be able to take part even behind NAT boxes.
  • An ADVPN MUST support L3VPNs running over the IPsec tunnels.

SHOULD-level items include seamless handoff of roaming endpoints, easy handoff of a session to another gateway, reportable and manageable SA changes, connecting endpoints of different organizations, administrator-chosen star, full-mesh or partial mesh topology, multicast scaling, monitoring and logging, per-peer QoS, and avoiding the hub as a single point of failure. Creating a MIB or other management technique is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The wish list says: adding a new office should not make every other office change its settings, secrets must stay secret, and the system should still work from behind home routers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document itself adds no new security concerns, but a solution might. RFC 4301 is silent on how the Security Policy Database (SPD) and Peer Authorization Database (PAD) are populated and implies they are static and set by a human. Letting a protocol update them dynamically changes the security policy that endpoints enforce, so it must be thought out carefully.

The RFC's example attack is traffic stealing: if an SPD entry says traffic to 192.0.2.10 goes through a gateway named Gw-Mallory, that gateway could impersonate or proxy the real site and read the traffic. Updates therefore need a clear trust model. Hubs can also be a single point of failure that cuts off the whole system.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could add a line to your address book saying send my mail through me, they could read it. Any automatic system has to be careful about who is allowed to change the list.
